lesson.title: Angles in triangles

lead.text: The last lesson showed that a straight line is a half-turn of 180°. The torn corners of the paper triangle fit along such a line, so together they make a half-turn too. Each corner of a triangle is an angle, and the three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. We call that total the angle sum of a triangle.

It holds for every triangle. A tall thin triangle has one very small angle and one very large one, and a wide flat triangle has a different mix. The total stays at 180° whatever the shape, because the torn corners would still lie flat along a line. The figure takes the corners off one triangle and sets them along a line.

afterFigure.text: So if you know two of the corners, the total fixes the third. First, try it on the torn triangle.

lead.text: Lay the three torn corners side by side along a straight edge.

Because the three angles add up to 180°, a missing angle is whatever is left after the known ones are taken away. Add the two you know and take the sum away from 180°. For a triangle with angles of 62° and 41°, the two add to 103°. Taking that from 180° leaves 77°, which is the third angle.

A quick check is to add all three at the end. They should come to 180°, and here 62° + 41° + 77° = 180°. The method works on any triangle where you can see two of the angles, so the next question has a triangle with two angles marked.

diagram.alt: A triangle with two corners of 62 and 41 degrees, and under it a straight line of 180 degrees split into the same two angles. The first view leaves the third corner unknown, and the second shows it is 77 degrees.
diagram.caption: The two known corners use up 103° of the straight line. What is left is the third corner.

lead.text: Two angles of this triangle are marked. The third corner fills what is left of the 180°.
One kind of triangle comes up so often that it has a name. A triangle with one right angle, a corner of 90°, is called a right triangle. The corner of a set square is one.

The angle sum tells you something about the other two corners. The right angle uses up 90° of the 180°, so the other two share the remaining 90°. If one of them is 20°, the other is 90° − 20° = 70°. The figure shows two right triangles, and in each the two angles that are not the right angle add to 90°.
Right triangles come back later in the course whenever distances need measuring, so it is worth knowing how their angles behave.
Find the third angle by taking both known angles from the total.
Some triangles have two angles of the same size. When two angles are equal and you know the third, the method gets one extra step.

Take the known angle away from 180° first. What remains has to be shared between the two equal angles, so each gets half of it. If the odd angle is 40°, then 180° − 40° = 140° remains, and half of that is 70° for each of the equal pair. Check the result: 70° + 70° + 40° = 180°.
So far every triangle we have met was a real one. The last question is whether any three numbers can be the angles of a triangle.

steps.headline: Which sets of angles are possible

lead.text: Any three positive numbers can be written down as angles, but only some sets are the corners of a real triangle. The test is the angle sum. If the three add up to exactly 180°, a triangle with those angles can be drawn. If they add up to more or to less, no triangle has those angles, because the torn corners would either run past the straight edge or leave a gap.

Angles of 30°, 60° and 90° can form a triangle, because they add to 180°. It is the right triangle again. Angles of 50°, 60° and 80° cannot, because they add to 190°. A corner with no turn is no corner at all, so every angle must also be greater than 0°.
Use that test on the next question.

diagram.alt: Three sets of angles laid end to end along a straight line of 180 degrees. 30, 60 and 90 fill it exactly, 50, 60 and 80 run past the end, and 40, 60 and 70 leave a gap.
diagram.caption: Lay the three angles end to end along the line. Only when they fill it exactly can they be the corners of a triangle.

lead.text: A student wants to draw a triangle with two right angles. Test the angles against the total before drawing.

lesson.orientation: Find a missing triangle angle and test whether angle measures are possible.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Cut a triangle out of paper. It can have any shape you like, tall and thin or short and wide. Tear off its three corners and lay them side by side on the table with their points touching.

The corners fit together along a straight edge, with no gap and no overlap. Try again with a different triangle and the same thing happens. In one triangle two of the corners measure 70° and 50°, and the third is too crumpled to measure.

It is odd that three corners of such different sizes should always fill a straight edge exactly. This lesson turns that fact into a tool. It gives you one rule that holds for every triangle, and a quick way to find a corner you cannot measure.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a missing angle in any triangle and tell whether three angles could make one.

recap.keyIdea: The three angles of a triangle add to 180°, so any missing angle is 180° minus the others.

blocks.text: You found that corners of 70° and 50° leave 60° of the straight edge for the third. After that you used the same subtraction on a right triangle and on a triangle with two equal angles.
You also used the total to rule out a triangle with two right angles.

recap.nextHook: Corners are only one thing to measure on a shape. Next, a room needs skirting board along its edge and tiles across its floor, and the two jobs call for different numbers.

questions.prompt: A triangle has angles 48° and 67°. What is its third angle in degrees?
hints: All three angles of a triangle together make 180°.
Add the two angles you are given.
Subtract 48 + 67 from 180.
questions.onCorrect: 65°. Take the two angles you know from 180°.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the two angles added. The third angle is what is left of 180°.
That leaves out the 67° angle. All three angles share the total.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has another angle of 32°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: The right angle uses half of the triangle's total.
The two acute angles add to 90°.
Calculate 90 − 32.
questions.onCorrect: 58°. Take the right angle and the 32° from 180°. The two sharp angles share 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: 90° is the right angle you already have. Find the third angle.
That leaves out the right angle. Take it from 180° as well.

questions.prompt: A triangle has two equal angles and a third angle of 44°. Find one of the equal angles in degrees.
hints: Take the unequal angle from 180°.
Split what remains equally between two angles.
Halve the leftover.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equal angles share 180 − 44 = 136°; each is 136/2 = 68°.

questions.onCorrect: 68°. The two equal angles share what the third leaves, so halve it.

misconceptions.feedback: 136° is what the two equal angles share. Each gets half of it.
44° is the third angle, which you were given. Find the equal pair.

hints: Add up what two right angles use.

acceptedIdeas: No, the third angle would have nothing left.

questions.prompt: A triangular sign has angles 39° and 86°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: Treat all three angles as parts of 180°.
Find the total of the two given angles.
Calculate 180 − (39 + 86).
questions.onCorrect: 55°. Whatever the shape, the other two angles leave 180° minus their sum.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 39 + 86. The third angle is what is left of 180°.
That leaves out the 86° angle. Take both known angles from 180°.

questions.prompt: Which set can be the interior angles of a triangle?
hints: Check both the total and whether every angle is positive.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180° and all three measures are positive.

questions.onCorrect: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180°. A triangle's angles must add to exactly 180°.

misconceptions.feedback: Those add to 210°, which is too much.
Those add to 190°, which is too much.

questions.prompt: Two corners of a paper triangle measure 70° and 50°. How big is the third corner, in degrees?
hints: Three corners fit side by side along a straight edge. How many degrees is a straight edge?
Add the two corners you know.
Take that total from the straight edge.
questions.onCorrect: 60°. The three corners fill a straight line, 180°, so the third is what the other two leave.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the two corners added together. The third corner is what is left of the straight line.
That leaves out the 50° corner. All three corners fill the line.

questions.prompt: Why do the other two angles add to 90°?
hints: How much of the 180° does the right angle already take?

acceptedIdeas: The right angle uses 90° of the 180°, so 90° is left for the other two.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The right angle uses 90° of the 180°, so 90° is left for the other two.

choices.label: The right angle uses 90° of the 180°, so 90° is left for the other two.
Every triangle has angles that add to 90°.

questions.onCorrect: The right angle uses 90° of the 180°. The other two angles share the 90° that is left.

misconceptions.feedback: The total is 180° for every triangle. The right angle is the part that uses up 90°.
They can differ, as long as they add up to 90°.

hints: The right angle uses 90°. How much of the 180° is left?
The two equal angles share what is left.

misconceptions.feedback: 90° is what the two angles share. Each gets half of it.
